Manufacturing Genius

By Srihith Jarabana One decision, one round, one prize October 2026

MANUFACTURING GENIUS

Srihith Jarabana

The last round

The rival always stays safe.

Rule 1 of 3

Your rival is stuck with a fixed rule here. Which row gives you the bigger expected share of the prize?

You (player A)105
Rival (player B)100

You lead.

Your share of the prize

Rival safe

Rival risky

Against this rival

Press a row to play one round. The higher final score wins; a tie splits the prize.

Let’s put you in the lead for a moment. You’re player A, there’s one decision left, and staying safe sounds reasonable enough. Your rival, however, gets the same choice. You both decide at the same time, so there’s no waiting to see what they do first. Pick safe or risky, then change the rival’s rule and try again. You might find that protecting a lead has quite a bit to do with the person behind you.

Here are the rules. Playing safe adds nothing. Playing risky adds either +10 or −10 on a coin flip. To begin with, if you both go risky, you get the same coin flip. Whoever finishes higher takes the prize, and a tie splits it. Nothing else counts: finishing on 115 instead of 106 gets you nothing extra.

One thing worth noticing: neither choice changes your score on average. Risky is +10 or −10 with even odds, so your expected score stays at 105 either way. What does change is your expected share of the prize, and that depends on what your rival picks too. (I count a tie as half a win throughout, which is why I talk about prize share instead of win probability. They aren’t quite the same number.)

The whole game in one table. Rows are your choices as A, columns are B’s, and each entry is your expected share of the prize, worked out by going through every possible coin flip.

A chooses B safe B risky
Safe 100% 50%
Risky 50% 100%

If you both pick the same thing, you keep your lead: either nobody moved, or you both moved by the same amount. If you pick different things, whoever went risky can flip the order. So you want to match your rival, and your rival wants to do whatever you didn’t. Neither of you can settle on a predictable move without the other one taking advantage of it.

The only stable answer is for both of you to randomize. In equilibrium you go risky 50.0% of the time, your rival goes risky 50.0% of the time, and your expected prize share works out to 75.0%. At those odds, neither of you can do better by switching on your own. This is for one round, played once, with both choices made at the same time. Any single game still ends in a win, a loss or a split; the percentages are what you’d get on average.

Correlation changes the game

Now give each risky player their own coin flip, so the shocks are independent. The both-risky entry drops to 75.0%, each player goes risky 66.7% of the time in equilibrium, and your expected share falls to 66.7%. It’s the same fair gamble on the menu, but matching your rival’s choice no longer means matching their result.

After the three guided rules, free play lets you move the lead, the correlation (negative values make the flips tend to go opposite ways) and your rival’s rule wherever you like, including ties and leads sitting right on the edge of what one flip can undo. Some settings have more than one equilibrium. The game shows one I’ve checked, and I’m not claiming it’s the only one.

One more thing, and everything after this depends on it: the two players in this game are equally good. Your five-point lead says nothing about skill. That’s the next problem.

What does a winner tell us?

Leaderboards make a complicated contest look rather simple (one name at the top, everyone else below). What they leave out is how the players chose to get there. If the prize depends on rank, taking a chance can actually be a sensible decision, even when it adds nothing to expected performance. So the winning score ends up saying something about the person and something about the game they were playing.

That’s the question I want to dig into: can a contest end up rewarding looking exceptional more reliably than actually being exceptional? The duel above was small enough to solve exactly. From here I’ll give the players real, lasting differences in ability and see who the game picks.

One note before the study: every number in here comes from either an exact calculation or a simulation I ran. None of it is real market or fund data.

Now give someone an actual edge

So far I’ve only asked who wins. The more interesting question is what winning tells you, and for that the players need to actually differ. In this part, one player is better than the other by δ\delta points per round (+δ/2+\delta/2 and −δ/2-\delta/2, assigned at random). That difference sticks around: it shows up in every round and in any test afterwards.

Each round adds noise on top of ability. A player’s first-round score and their final two-round score are:

Si=θi+σ0Zi.Fi=Si+θi+abiXi.S_i=\theta_i+\sigma_0Z_i. \qquad F_i=S_i+\theta_i+a b_iX_i.

Here bib_i is 0 for safe and 1 for risky, XiX_i is a fair ±1 coin flip, and aa is the size of the gamble. The two players’ flips have correlation ρ\rho and have nothing to do with the first-round noise. Going risky spreads your score out. It doesn’t make you any better, and it doesn’t raise your expected score.

I’m being generous to the players here. Each of them knows both abilities and both first-round scores. The judge (I’ll call them the evaluator) never sees ability and simply picks whoever has the higher final score, with a coin flip for ties. I don’t think real competitors can read each other’s talent this well. It’s a simplification that lets me solve every last round exactly.

Because the players know the abilities, what matters going into the last round is the effective gap, d=SA−SB+θA−θBd=S_A-S_B+\theta_A-\theta_B: the current lead plus the edge in ability that’s about to show up again in round two. The visible lead on its own isn’t enough. From there, each last round is the same kind of game as the duel above, and I solve each one exactly.

Then I compare strategic risk-taking (the equilibrium) against two simple rules that just tell players what to do: both safe, where nobody’s allowed to gamble, and both risky, where everybody has to. Those two are benchmarks, not something the players would choose themselves. I locked in 48 parameter settings, with 10,000 independent contests each, before looking at any results. Noise in the first round and in the later test both have a standard deviation of 1 point.

Same gamble, opposite answers

This is the part I find most interesting. Hold ability and the size of the gamble fixed, and only change whether the risky players share one coin flip or get their own. Compared with forcing everyone to gamble, strategic choice goes from picking the better player more often to picking them less often. Compared with making everyone play safe, it’s worse either way.

Why does it flip? With independent flips, forcing both players to gamble means a lead of up to twice the gamble’s size can get wiped out (one goes up, the other goes down). Left to choose, a leader who’s ahead by more than one gamble’s worth just plays safe, and the lead can’t be caught. Close contests change too, but at this setting the net effect is that the better player gets picked more often than under both-risky.

With one shared flip, forcing both players to gamble moves both scores by the same amount, so the ranking never changes and it’s identical to both-safe. Strategic play is different. In close contests the players randomize, and sometimes only one of them ends up taking the risk. That can flip the ranking, and under these assumptions it lowers how often the better player gets picked overall.

Why both-safe can’t be beaten

I want to be upfront about this: the comparison with both-safe was never going to come out the other way. Under these assumptions, letting players choose risk can’t pick the better player more often than making everyone play safe. That’s a mathematical fact about the setup, and the simulation only measures how big the gap is.

Here’s the intuition. From the better player’s side, the effective gap is G∼N(2δ,2σ02)G\sim N(2\delta,2\sigma_0^2) (the second number is the variance). It’s centred above zero, so they’re more likely to be ahead by any given amount than behind by it. Risk cuts both ways: sometimes it knocks the better player out of a lead they deserved, and sometimes it rescues them from a deficit they didn’t. Since the better player is more often the one in front, the knock-outs outnumber the rescues. It also helps the safe rule that a safe second round is a clean, noise-free read on ability, and that risk in this model doesn’t produce anything useful.

The maths

Exact formulas, for anyone who wants them

Write V(g)V(g) for the equilibrium probability of winning at effective gap gg. Label symmetry gives V(−g)=1−V(g)V(-g)=1-V(g), and safe wins exactly when g>0g>0 outside zero-probability ties. If ff is the density of GG, then

Aeq−Asafe=−∫0∞[1−V(g)][f(g)−f(−g)]dg≤0.A_{\mathrm{eq}}-A_{\mathrm{safe}} =-\int_0^\infty[1-V(g)][f(g)-f(-g)]\,dg\leq0.

For δ>0\delta>0, f(g)>f(−g)f(g)>f(-g) at positive gg, while V(g)≤1V(g)\leq1. For a>0a>0, away from the boundaries, V(g)V(g) equals one for g>ag>a, v=(2+ρ)/(3+ρ)v=(2+\rho)/(3+\rho) for 0<g<a0<g<a, 1−v1-v for −a<g<0-a<g<0, and zero for g<−ag<-a. The leader can guarantee victory by staying safe at g>ag>a, even when both-risky could still overturn the lead.

Let CC be the CDF of GG. Exact accuracy is

Aeq=1−C(a)+v[C(a)−C(0)]+(1−v)[C(0)−C(−a)],A_{\mathrm{eq}}=1-C(a)+v[C(a)-C(0)]+(1-v)[C(0)-C(-a)],

while Asafe=1−C(0)A_{\mathrm{safe}}=1-C(0). For both-risky, substitute 2a2a for aa and (3+ρ)/4(3+\rho)/4 for vv. At zero risk every rule agrees. The continuous-noise formulas ignore only probability-zero boundaries; the discrete tests use the original tie-aware enumerator. Numerically integrating the enumerated games checks these formulas independently.

Every setting, charted

Selection accuracy and paired differences

Meet the winner again

Picking a winner is only half of it. The other half is what you see when you look at them again. So after the contest, I keep everyone’s ability the same and test both players one more time with fresh, independent noise: Hi=θi+σHEiH_i=\theta_i+\sigma_HE_i. Nobody gets to gamble on this one, and these new scores never feed back into who won.

Start with the winning score itself. Per round, how far above their real ability does the winner’s score sit? I’ll call that gap overstatement. It isn’t a measure of anyone lying or cheating. It’s what happens when you pick the higher of two noisy numbers: even if both players were equally good, the winner would still tend to look better than they are.

Then compare the winner’s per-round score from the contest, F/2F/2, with how they do on the fresh test, HH. Part of the drop is just luck not repeating. Part of it is that the fresh test runs under different rules (no gamble, new noise). Calling the whole thing “regression to the mean” skips over that second part.

In the independent-flip example, the equilibrium winner scores 0.529 points per round on average, but their actual ability averages 0.210. That’s an overstatement of 0.318 [0.307, 0.330] points. On the fresh test they average 0.207 [0.187, 0.228] points, in line with their real ability. Brackets are 95% Monte Carlo intervals.

These numbers aren’t independent of each other. With unequal abilities, E[θselected]=δ[P(correct)−1/2]E[\theta_{\mathrm{selected}}]=\delta[P(\text{correct})-1/2], and in the simulation that holds exactly for the sample means too. Because the fresh noise is independent, E[Hselected]=E[θselected]E[H_{\mathrm{selected}}]=E[\theta_{\mathrm{selected}}]. So selection accuracy, the winner’s ability and their fresh performance are really the same finding measured three ways. What the fresh test does is make the gap between a great result and a great player easy to see.

When the players are equally able, there’s no “better” player, so accuracy doesn’t mean anything. The winner’s average ability is zero by construction, but their score still overstates it. And with no gamble at all, all three rules pick exactly the same people. I’ve kept these controls in the full results below.

Every setting, overstatement and fresh test

Every ability gap and correlation

What I think this actually shows

The comparison matters a lot here. Under these assumptions, letting players choose their risk can’t pick the better player more often than making them both play safe. The setup decides that direction; the simulation only tells you how big the difference is. Compare strategic choice with making everybody gamble, though, and it can come out better or worse. It would be pretty easy to blur those two together and walk away with a much bigger claim than the model supports, so I’m trying hard not to.

A winner doesn’t have to cheat, or even misjudge the odds, to end up with a score that overstates their ability. They can understand the rules perfectly and play them well. The prize is for coming first, after all. The trouble starts when the evaluator asks that same result to tell them who’s actually better at the underlying thing, because those aren’t quite the same question. I think that gap is worth paying attention to, but this study can’t tell you how big it is at any real firm, fund or hiring panel.

Before anyone takes this as an argument against risk, look at what risk is allowed to do here: nothing. It adds no expected performance. Nobody learns anything, works harder, or takes on a project that only pays off if someone is willing to gamble on it. The safe rule gets a clean second read on ability, and the players know things about each other that the evaluator can’t see. Those assumptions are generous to playing safe, and they’re the reason the conclusion has to stay attached to this particular game.

Read the record with the rules attached

So before reading a winner’s score as proof of ‘exceptional’ ability, ask a few things. What choices did the contest reward? What could the rival do? Does the result hold up when everyone is tested again under the same rules? None of that makes a leaderboard useless. It just makes the rules behind it part of the evidence.

Methods, sources and reproduction

Published research. Hvide and Kristiansen look at contests where players choose how much risk to take (instead of how hard to work) and ask how well those contests pick out the best player (Hvide and Kristiansen 2003). Chen, Hughson and Stoughton study strategic risk-taking in multi-period mutual fund tournaments; their abstract describes leaders cutting back on risk depending on how far ahead they are (Chen et al. 2025). These papers are the background for this piece. My model and my numbers don’t come from either of them.

I also read earlier working versions of both: the Norges Bank paper (series 1999/2, text dated February 2000) and the SSRN manuscript (May 2018). I checked their model sections and conclusions and verified the final journal details and abstracts, but I haven’t read the full published versions. I don’t borrow any empirical estimate or proof from either one.

What’s mine. The playable duel and its exact solutions are toy models I built for this piece. The ability study is new synthetic analysis under the assumptions above. It isn’t a replication of either paper, none of it is real financial data, and it can’t tell you how hiring panels, funds, managers or markets actually behave.

How it’s computed. Seed 20261025 starts separate PCG64 random streams for labels, first scores, potential risky shocks, action draws, tie breaks and the fresh test, with independent streams for each parameter setting. All three rules share the same underlying draws within each replicate, so policy differences are paired comparisons. Every original state maps to one of finitely many exact payoff matrices, and every equilibrium I report passes a unilateral-deviation check. When a game has more than one pure saddle point, the solver takes the first in safe/risky row-major order. The game’s value doesn’t depend on that choice, but the selected exposures and overstatement can. No general-sum preferences or alternative rewards are added.

Uncertainty. Accuracy uses Wilson intervals. Means and paired differences use the sample standard deviation over the square root of the replicate count, with normal intervals. Every interval is a pointwise, approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval. They measure simulation error inside this model, and say nothing about whether the model fits any real institution. I’ve left small fluctuations between settings and overlapping intervals as they came out.

Settings and how to rerun everything

Study settings and reproduction commands
Setting Value
design_version 1.0
replicates 10000
master_seed 20261025
sigma_0 1.0
sigma_H 1.0
delta [0.0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.5]
risk_size [0.0, 0.5, 1.5, 3.0]
correlation [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]

From a clean checkout, create a project environment, install requirements-lock.txt, then install this package with --no-deps -e .. Use that environment’s Python for the commands below, and point QUARTO_PYTHON at it before rendering. The README has the full Windows and macOS/Linux steps.

python scripts/check.py
python scripts/export_reference.py
node scripts/check_browser_math.cjs
python scripts/run_study.py
python scripts/make_figures.py
quarto render index.qmd
You end up with a single self-contained _output/index.html. It doesn’t need a server or make any data requests. The coin flips in the game use your browser’s randomness for one illustrative play; the exact expectations and study results don’t depend on it.

References

Chen, Joseph, Eric Hughson, and Neal Stoughton. 2025. “Strategic Mutual Fund Tournaments.” Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 60 (7): 3344–79. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109024000590.
Hvide, Hans K., and Eirik Gaard Kristiansen. 2003. “Risk Taking in Selection Contests.” Games and Economic Behavior 42 (1): 172–79. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0899-8256(02)00538-9.

Set in Ultra, League Gothic and Old Standard. Masthead engraving from Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper, 1879, via the Library of Congress. Paper texture from a photograph by Pink Sherbet Photography, CC BY 2.0, cropped and tinted. Every number on this sheet is recomputed from the saved study when the page is built.
